walkthroughs.body_html:
Global Development & Connections (Health, Human Rights / Migration, Identity) — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Global Development & Connections (Health, Human Rights / Migration, Identity) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Global Development & Connections (Health, Human Rights / Migration, Identity).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A refugee is best defined as someone who:
options: Flees across a border owing to a well-founded fear of persecution or conflict
Moves abroad mainly to earn higher wages
Moves to another region within their own country
Travels abroad temporarily for tourism

mcqs.q: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in:
Which is an example of 'hard power' intervention?
options: Military action
Cultural influence through films and media
Educational exchange programmes
Diplomatic persuasion

mcqs.q: Is development the same as economic growth?
options: No — growth means rising GDP, while development also includes health, education, rights and quality of life; an economy can grow while wellbeing stagnates.
Development means a country is physically growing in land area.
A country with rising GDP is automatically becoming more developed.
Migrants are people who travel abroad on holiday.
Migrants are people who travel abroad on holiday.
Almost all migration is forced displacement caused by war.
No — the majority of international migrants move for work, study or family reasons; refugees fleeing persecution are a minority of total migrant flows.
Development means a country is physically growing in land area.

mcqs.q: Does signing a human-rights treaty guarantee rights are protected?
options: No — ratification creates legal commitments, but enforcement depends on national governments, courts and political will, so practice often lags far behind paper commitments.
Development means a country is physically growing in land area.
Once a country signs a treaty, abuses stop.
Human-rights treaties only apply to island nations.
